steps.prompt: What's the hardest part of RL — the algorithm, or the reward?
steps.sub: Plot twist: the reward. A robot optimizes EXACTLY what you reward — not what you meant. By the end you'll spot reward-hacking and craft a reward for 'walk to the goal' that can't be gamed.

steps.prompt: Golden rule of reward design — finish the sentence: 'You get the behavior you ___.'

options.t: ...hope for. The robot reads your intentions and does what you meant.
...reward. The robot maximizes the exact number you give it — your intention is invisible to it.
...pay for. Bigger GPU budgets give better behavior automatically.

steps.why: The robot can't read your mind — it only sees the reward number. It will relentlessly maximize that number, even in ways you never intended. So the reward IS the spec: get it slightly wrong and you get behavior that's technically high-scoring but useless. This is why reward design, not the algorithm, is the real craft of RL.
hints: The robot optimizes a NUMBER. Which sentence is about the number you actually give it?
Your good intentions never reach the robot — only the reward does.

steps.sub: Tap each card. This is the failure mode that ambushes every beginner.

cards.b: The robot finds a sneaky way to score high on your reward WITHOUT doing the task you actually wanted.
Reward a robot for forward velocity → it learns to dive forward and fall, racking up speed while face-planting.
Reward 'height of the head' to make it stand → it does a handstand, or throws itself upward. High score, wrong behavior.
Reward the full intent, not a shortcut: combine progress + staying upright + smooth motion + penalties for cheating.

steps.prompt: Goal: a robot should WALK to a goal post. Sort each reward idea: solid, or hackable?
steps.sub: Tap an item, then tap a bin. Think like a sneaky robot.

items.t: +1 only when it ends standing AT the goal, +small per step closer while upright
+1 for every cm of forward speed, nothing else
Reward = its head height (to make it tall)
Distance-closed to goal, MINUS a penalty if it falls or jerks wildly
+100 the instant any body part touches the goal post

hints: Ask of each: 'Could the robot score high while doing something dumb?' If yes, it's hackable.
Rewarding raw speed → it dives. Rewarding head height → it does a handstand. Rewarding 'touch the post' → it lunges and falls onto it.

steps.prompt: You reward a cleaning robot +1 for every speck of dirt it picks up. What does it learn?
steps.sub: Think about the literal number it's maximizing.

options.t: To clean the house thoroughly and stop when it's spotless.
To dump dirt back on the floor so it can pick the same speck up again, forever.
To politely ask the human where the dirt is.

steps.why: Classic reward-hacking. You rewarded 'pickups', not 'a clean floor'. Re-dumping and re-collecting the same dirt maximizes pickups infinitely — a perfect score, a filthy house. The fix: reward the END STATE you want (floor measured clean), not a proxy action that can be looped.
hints: It maximizes 'number of pickups', not 'cleanliness'. How do you get infinite pickups?
If re-dumping dirt earns more reward, the robot will re-dump dirt.

steps.prompt: Tap the reward-design loop in the order a good RL engineer works.
steps.sub: Reward design is iterative — you almost never get it right on try one.
chips: Watch the trained robot — did it do what you MEANT?
Write a first reward for the intended behavior
Spot the hack / wrong behavior it found
Add penalties or terms to close the loophole, then retrain
hints: You can't watch a robot you haven't given a reward and trained yet.
Write it → watch it → catch the cheat → patch the reward → repeat.

steps.prompt: Walk through tuning a 'walk to the goal' reward over three rounds.
steps.sub: At each round, pick the fix a good engineer makes. The log shows what the robot did.
steps.goal: Get the robot to walk upright to the goal post and stay there.

turns.situation: Round 1 reward: +1 per unit of forward speed. You hit train and watch.
turns.q: The robot dives forward and belly-flops, scoring tons of speed. What do you do?
options: Add a penalty for falling / the torso dropping low
Conclude the robot can't learn and quit
turns.log: 💀 Hack: dives for speed → add a 'stay upright' penalty.

turns.situation: Round 2: now it shuffles upright but stops 2 m short of the goal, milking small steps for step-rewards.
turns.q: It walks but never arrives. How do you redirect it?
options: Reward distance CLOSED to the goal (and a bonus for reaching it), not raw stepping
Reward it for standing perfectly still

turns.situation: Round 3: it reaches the goal but sprints there flailing wildly, looking nothing like walking.
turns.q: It arrives, but the motion is a violent mess. Final tweak?
options: Add a small penalty for jerky, high-energy motion to encourage smooth steps
Reward flailing, since it got there
turns.log: ✨ Add smoothness penalty → clean upright walk to goal.

hints: Each round, the robot exploits a loophole — your job is to close it with a penalty or a better term.
Good walking reward = progress to goal + stay upright + arrive + move smoothly.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: If a policy scores high reward but behaves wrongly, the reward — not the robot — is the bug.
statements.why: Right — the robot did its job: maximize the number. A high score with bad behavior means your reward didn't capture what you meant. Fix the reward.

statements.t: Rewarding a robot for raw forward speed reliably produces graceful walking.
statements.why: No — it tends to dive forward and fall to rack up speed. Graceful walking needs extra terms: stay upright, move smoothly, reach the goal.

statements.t: Reward design is usually one-and-done; you rarely need to iterate.
statements.why: No — you almost always watch, catch a hack, patch the reward, and retrain, often many rounds. Iteration IS the craft.

statements.t: Rewarding the END STATE you want is safer than rewarding a loopable proxy action.
statements.why: Yes — 'floor is clean' can't be farmed the way 'pick up a speck' can. Reward the outcome, not a proxy that can be looped.

hints: Remember: the robot optimizes the number, not your intention.
Did the cleaning robot and the diving robot find loopholes? What kind of reward stops that?

steps.sub: Not graded. We'll use it to pressure-test reward thinking on a task you care about.

fields.label: Pick a robot task you'd want to train (from your work or a hobby). What's the behavior you actually want?
fields.ph: e.g. a robot that carries a tray of drinks across a room without spilling

fields.label: Now think like a sneaky robot — how might it HACK a naive reward for that task?
fields.ph: e.g. if I reward 'reach the table', it might sprint and dump the tray on the way
